## Learning goals

By the end of this page:

- I can compare fonts instead of choosing the first one I like.
- I can zoom out to test whether a design stays clear.
- I can use contrast, labels, and open letter shapes.
- I can write useful alt text for a shared image.

## Why this is useful

Accessible design helps more people see, read, and understand your work. It also makes signs, labels, slides, and graphics work better for everyone.

## What you will test

Use these checks with a nameplate, logo, slide, poster, label, diagram, or web graphic.

## Before you start

Open the design you want to test. Keep an editable copy so you can change the font, size, spacing, and colours.

## 1. Compare several fonts

Try the same word in at least three fonts. Change only the font at first.

<picture>
  <source media="(max-width: 600px)" srcset="../../assets/name-tag-photopea/lesson-1-nameplate/font-choice-comparison-mobile.svg">
  <img src="../../assets/name-tag-photopea/lesson-1-nameplate/font-choice-comparison.svg" alt="Four versions of Andrade compare serif, sans serif, rounded display, and script fonts. Sans serif is shown as a strong starting point, while notes identify engraving and readability risks in the other styles." style="display:block;width:100%;height:auto">
</picture>

- **Serif:** Georgia and Times New Roman have small finishing strokes. Serif fonts are common in printed books. Thin strokes may disappear when a design is made.
- **Sans serif:** DejaVu Sans, Arial, Verdana, and Open Sans use simpler letter shapes. They are a strong starting point for signs, screens, and nameplates.
- **Rounded or display:** Nunito, Montserrat, and Impact add personality. Check for crowded letters and closed inside spaces.
- **Script or decorative:** Brush Script and similar fonts can feel personal. Joined or detailed letters can be hard to read.

No font is always good or bad. Choose one that fits the job and stays easy to read.

## 2. Zoom out before choosing

A font may look clear while it fills the screen. Zoom out until you can see the whole design.

<picture>
  <source media="(max-width: 600px)" srcset="../../assets/accessible-design/font-zoom-test-mobile.svg">
  <img src="../../assets/accessible-design/font-zoom-test.svg" alt="Andrade appears in four font styles at a large size and again inside a small nameplate at about twenty-five percent size. The sans serif version remains the quickest to read." style="display:block;width:100%;height:auto">
</picture>

In Photopea:

1. Press **Ctrl + -** on Windows or **Command + -** on a Mac.
2. Stop near `25%` or when the whole canvas fits on the screen.
3. Read the design without leaning closer.
4. Ask which font you can recognize first.
5. Zoom back in to check line quality before exporting.

Also step back from the screen or read the design from an arm's length away. If you need extra time to recognize the word, try a simpler font, larger type, or more spacing.

## 3. Use four accessibility checks

Use the checks below before you export or publish.

<picture>
  <source media="(max-width: 600px)" srcset="../../assets/name-tag-photopea/lesson-1-nameplate/accessible-design-checks-mobile.svg">
  <img src="../../assets/name-tag-photopea/lesson-1-nameplate/accessible-design-checks.svg" alt="Four accessible-design checks show strong contrast, labels used with colour, open letter shapes with sturdy lines, and a short alt text description for a shared image." style="display:block;width:100%;height:auto">
</picture>

1. **Use strong contrast.** Dark text on a light background, or light text on a dark background, is usually easier to read. For text shared online, aim for at least `4.5:1`, or `3:1` for large text.
2. **Do not use colour alone.** Add a label, shape, pattern, or icon when colour carries meaning.
3. **Keep letters open.** Use lines that are thick enough to print, cut, or engrave. Keep the spaces inside `a`, `e`, and `o` visible.
4. **Describe digital images.** Add short alt text that explains what another person needs to understand.

## 4. Keep text clear over images

Text can disappear when it sits on a busy photo or changing video.

- Put a solid, high-contrast box behind important text.
- Use an outline or shadow only when it makes every letter clearer.
- Avoid heavy 3D effects that change the letter shapes.
- Check the lightest and darkest parts of the background.

A solid background is often more reliable than adding several effects.

## 5. Test with another person

Show the design without explaining it first.

Ask:

- What did you read first?
- Which part was hard to see?
- What did the colours, shapes, or icons mean?
- What would make the design easier to understand?

Use the answer as evidence. Change one thing, then test again.

## Check your work

Your design is ready when:

- the main words are easy to read when zoomed out;
- similar characters such as `I`, `l`, and `1` are easy to tell apart;
- lines are thick enough for the final material or screen;
- text and background have strong contrast;
- colour is not the only way information is shown; and
- important digital images have useful alt text.

## Common issues

- **The font looks good up close but disappears when zoomed out:** use a simpler or heavier font.
- **Letters close up:** reduce boldness, add spacing, or choose more open letter shapes.
- **Text disappears over a photo:** add a solid high-contrast background behind it.
- **A colour change carries all the meaning:** add a label, icon, shape, or pattern.
- **Alt text repeats every detail:** describe only what a person needs to understand in this context.

::: {.ter-curriculum-relevance}
**Design curriculum:** Use this guide while creating logos, nameplates, slides, posters, labels, diagrams, and digital interfaces. Accessibility is part of testing and improving a design.
:::

You compared font choices, tested them while zoomed out, checked contrast and letter shapes, used more than colour, and planned useful alt text.
